title: History / Timeline
text:
Date
Event
Source




1948 or 1949 [conflicting sources]
Original El Cerrito Library constructed at 6510 Stockton Avenue. One source (the Feb. 2026 Impact Report) states 1948; a separate September 2026 Task Force presentation states 1949. Not yet resolved.
Impact Report, 2/19/2026, p.3; Sept. 8, 2026 Task Force Presentation, p.13


1960
Library expanded to ~6,500 sq ft.
Impact Report, p.3


2002
City begins actively evaluating sites for a new library (Portola Middle School site, Civic Theater site, Community Center, San Pablo Ave sites, current site).
Impact Report, p.3–4; Agenda Bill 8.B, 1/20/2026


2006
City retains independent experts; first comprehensive Library Needs Assessment + Building Program completed, sized at ~21,000 sq ft, prepared to pursue a state construction bond grant.
Impact Report, p.3


2006 (Nov.)
Statewide bond measure that would have funded the grant program fails at the ballot.
Impact Report, p.3


2013
City Council adopts Strategic Plan identifying the library as a priority.
Impact Report, p.3; Nov. 21, 2023 presentation timeline slide


2014 (March)
City retains Kathryn Page Associates; updated Needs Assessment presented to Council, recommending ~20,845 sq ft.
Impact Report, p.3


2015
Strategic Plan updated; site options and cost models developed for a possible ballot measure.
Impact Report, p.4; Nov. 21, 2023 timeline slide


June 2, 2015
Godbe Research poll reported to Council: 72% of respondents favorable to a $30M library bond (40.9% “definitely yes,” 30.6% “probably yes”); poll of 418 online + 203 phone respondents in March 2015. Up from 69% support in a 2013 poll.
Times Herald, “El Cerrito poll finds strong support for new library,” 6/4/2015


July 19, 2016
City Council unanimously votes to place a $30 million library bond measure (Measure B) on the November 2016 ballot; also authorizes MOU with BART (Resolution 2016-68) to study TOD/library feasibility at the Plaza Station.
MOU BART library cc1608167.pdf; Impact Report p.4; Agenda Bill 8.A p.2


July 12, 2016
City’s Financial Advisory Board votes 3-1 to recommend ballot language explicitly disclose the measure as “a tax on real estate”; recommendation is not incorporated into the final ballot language adopted July 19.
East Bay Times editorial, 10/9/2016


Aug. 16, 2016
Agenda Bill formalizing MOU with BART for TOD/library feasibility study presented to Council.
MOU BART library cc1608167.pdf


Nov. 8, 2016
Measure B (2016): $30M library bond. Required 66.67% supermajority. Received 63% “Yes” (Impact Report) — reported elsewhere as 64% by a public commenter [conflicting figures in the record]. Fell short by ~500 votes.
Impact Report, p.4; public comment of Georgina Edwards, 11/21/2023 packet


2018
AB 2923 takes effect, requiring minimum zoning on BART-owned parcels.
Nov. 21, 2023 timeline slide


2018
MOU between City and BART (authorized 2016) formally executed.
Impact Report, p.29; Agenda Bill 8.A


2018–2019
El Cerrito Plaza Existing Conditions Report, BART Access Survey, and Parking Management Case Studies prepared.
Impact Report, p.29


Nov. 19, 2019
City Council adopts El Cerrito Plaza TOD Goals & Objectives, including “exploring options for integrating a public library into the TOD”; also requests (Resolution 2019-66) that BART include a potential library in its RFQ.
Impact Report, p.29; Agenda Bill 8.A; Nov. 21, 2023 timeline slide


2019
Library Workshop held to discuss proposed sites & partnerships.
Nov. 21, 2023 timeline slide


July 2020
BART initiates RFQ process, inviting developers to submit two conceptual site plans — one with a library, one without.
Impact Report, p.29


Nov. 2020
Developer team of Related California, Holliday Development, and SAHA selected; BART enters Exclusive Negotiating Agreement.
Impact Report, p.29; Nov. 21, 2023 timeline slide


2020
BART adopts El Cerrito Plaza TOD Goals & Objectives (later amended 2021).
Agenda Bill 8.A


2021–2023
TOD pre-planning: access planning, public engagement, library-specific public meetings, site planning.
Nov. 21, 2023 timeline slide


Oct. 3, 2022
Developer submits SB 330/AB 2923 application for the first TOD parcel, ahead of the SPASP update.
Agenda Bill 8.A


Dec. 6, 2022
San Pablo Avenue Specific Plan (SPASP) updated.
Agenda Bill 8.A


Dec. 2023
City’s Strategic Plan 2024–2029 adopted, articulating a goal to “Create a community hub anchored by the Plaza Transit-Oriented Development and a new Library.”
Agenda Bill 8.B, 1/20/2026


May 2023
Godbe Research poll (Tier 1 messaging ~59–60% support depending on statement).
Ira Sharenow letter, 11/19/2023, citing “May 2023 Survey: 60% YES; 34% NO”


Sept./Oct. 2023
Second Godbe poll round; full support figures not publicly disclosed per a CPRA request (see Cost & Funding History).
Ira Sharenow letter to City Clerk, 11/19/2023


Sept. 27, 2023
El Cerrito Library Public Forum held.
el-cerrito.org/library timeline


Nov. 21, 2023
Council study session (Item 9B) on the Plaza TOD library option; presentation identifies the library site as “Phase 4” of the TOD master plan; Council opts to explore a 2025 (rather than March 2024) ballot measure. Public comment from Al Miller, Michael Fischer, Georgina Edwards, Greg Lyman, Charles Taylor, and Ira Sharenow.
November 21 2023 presentation.pdf


2024–2025
Site plan finalized: library located on ground floor of a future affordable-housing building at Fairmount Ave & Liberty St, “Parcel C West.” Half-acre public plaza and potential café also part of TOD Master Plan.
Impact Report, p.29–30


June 11, 2024
City holds a Community Library Workshop at the El Cerrito Library.
el-cerrito.org/library timeline


April 1, 2025
City executes Consulting Services Agreement with Griffin Structures (Owner’s Representative) for Library Project services.
Griffin Structures Inc. Agreement, 2025.06.30, p.2–3


May 6, 2025
Citizen proponents file a Notice of Intent to Circulate an Initiative Petition (“The El Cerrito Library Initiative”) with the City Clerk.
Agenda Bill 8.A, 1/20/2026, p.1; elcerrito.gov/1753


May 21, 2025
City Attorney (Sky Woodruff) provides the Ballot Title and Summary, starting the 180-day circulation clock.
Agenda Bill 8.A, p.1


June 13–17, 2025
Proponents file a revised measure text; City Attorney issues a revised Ballot Title and Summary on June 17, 2025, restarting the 180-day circulation period.
Agenda Bill 8.A, p.1


June 27, 2025
Griffin Structures proposal for Owner’s Rep services through Sept. 2025, including DA negotiation support and Council presentation prep.
Griffin Structures Inc. 2025.06.30.1.pdf


Nov. 20, 2025
Signed petitions submitted to City Clerk (2,454 signatures per the Clerk’s prima facie count, prior to verification).
Agenda Bill 8.A, p.1; Certificate of Petition


Dec. 1, 2025
Petition deemed “filed” following City Clerk’s Prima Facie review.
Agenda Bill 8.A, p.1


Dec. 16, 2025
Council installs Gabe Quinto as Mayor for 2026 (AG Rob Bonta administers oath); library tax measure discussed informally at the reception.
ECCRG blog, referencing 12/16/2025 meeting


Jan. 9, 2026
Contra Costa County Elections confirms the petition contains sufficient valid signatures — 2,177 qualifying signatures after verification.
Agenda Bill 8.A, p.1; City Clerk’s Certificate of Petition; Sept. 8, 2026 Task Force Presentation


Jan. 20, 2026
Council adopts Resolution 2026-04, accepting the Certificate of Petition; Council requests a §9212 Impact Report and holds a study session (Item 8.B) on the current facility and five conceptual scenarios ($10M–$48M range).
Impact Report, p.2; Agenda Bill 8.A & 8.B, 1/20/2026


Feb. 6, 2026
Strategic Growth Council (SGC) staff (Justin DeWaele) advise, in an email later forwarded to Council, that AHSC Round 10 is likely to open March 2026 with a May/June 2026 deadline — undercutting the stated rationale that a June election would help a Parcel C West AHSC application.
SGC letter forwarded to council.docx


Feb. 17, 2026
Council adopts Resolution 2026-11, formally creating the El Cerrito Library Task Force (advisory; 7 voting residents incl. 1 youth member, 1-year terms, plus 3 non-voting invitees).
elcerrito.gov/1768/Library-Task-Force


Feb. 19, 2026
Special Council meeting: staff present the §9212 Impact Report; Council votes 4-1 (Ktsanes dissenting) to call a special election for June 2, 2026, adopting Resolution 2026-12. Wysinger urges the Council to stop “analysis and paralysis”; Ktsanes argues November would be cheaper/more democratic; Quinto confirms election costs would be reimbursed if the measure passes.
Impact Report, p.2; Contra Costa News, 3/10/2026; elcerrito.gov/1753


March 9, 2026
Contra Costa Registrar of Voters randomly assigns ballot letters; the El Cerrito measure becomes Measure C.
elcerrito.gov/1753


March 12, 2026
City Attorney Sky Woodruff signs the official Impartial Analysis of Measure C.
contracostavote.gov/m9002-en


March 18, 2026
Deadline for primary ballot arguments (for/against).
elcerrito.gov/1753; Contra Costa News, 3/10/2026


March 23, 2026
Deadline for rebuttal arguments.
Same as above


April 7, 2026
Council holds a study session on proposed exemptions to Measure C’s parcel tax; directs staff to return with a resolution clarifying/loosening exemption qualification requirements.
el-cerrito.org/library timeline


May 4, 2026
Vote-by-mail ballots mailed.
ca-elcerrito2.civicplus.com/217/Elections


June 2, 2026
ELECTION DAY. Measure C on the ballot as part of the California Statewide Direct Primary Election.
Multiple sources


June 2, 2026 (result)
Measure C failed. YES 3,264 (30.39%) — NO 7,475 (69.61%) of 10,739 total votes. Turnout 62.77%. See Measure C for the certified Statement of Results.
Certificate of the City of El Cerrito, City Clerk, dated July 21, 2026


August 2026
City states publicly that no dedicated library funding has been identified.
City’s library webpage, elcerrito.gov/library


Sept. 8, 2026
First Library Task Force meeting scheduled, 6:00 p.m., City Council Chambers — presents five post-election alternatives (renovate, renovate/expand, Plaza TOD, new standalone site, renovate a purchased building) since no dedicated funding source has been identified.
Sept. 8, 2026 Task Force Agenda, Presentation


2028 (projected)
Construction of “Phase 6” (the building slated to house the library, if funded) is not expected to begin before 2028 per the City’s TOD phasing information; City must execute a Development Agreement with the TOD developer by March 2027.
el-cerrito.org/library; Impact Report, p.32–33




Note on TOD phase numbering: the library building’s phase number in the TOD master plan has changed more than once across City documents — “Phase 4” in the Nov. 2023 presentation and the Feb. 2026 SGC letter, “Phase 6” on the City’s current library webpage. This reflects the TOD master plan being renumbered multiple times, not a single discrepancy to resolve.

title: Measure C
text:
Citizen-initiated ordinance adding Chapter 4.58 to the El Cerrito Municipal Code, authorizing an annual special parcel tax. (Impact Report, p.6)

Maximum initial rate: $0.17 per square foot of improvements; $100 per vacant parcel. (Impact Report, p.6; §4.58.040(A))
Annual escalator: up to the greater of Bay Area CPI or CA per-capita personal income growth, at Council’s discretion (not automatic). (Impact Report, p.6; §4.58.040(B))
Secondary statutory cap: total annual levy may not exceed 115% of revenue needed for (1) construction-debt service and (2) library operating costs for the first 10 years post-construction. (Impact Report, p.6–7; §4.58.040(C))
Use of funds: planning, permitting, environmental review, construction, and furnishing of a new library, plus up to 10 years of City library operating costs. (Impact Report, p.6–7; §4.58.060(A))
Duration: 30 years from the initial issuance of bonds for the library. (Impact Report, p.11; §4.58.110)
Projected gross annual revenue at maximum rates: $3,156,019 (rounded publicly to “~$3.1M”), based on 18,458,937 taxable building sq ft + 180 vacant parcels, FY2025-26 property profile. (Impact Report, p.18)
Average residential parcel: 1,946 sq ft → ~$331 projected initial annual tax. (Impact Report, p.18)
Exemptions: owners qualifying for the state’s Gonzalez-Deukmejian-Petris Senior Citizen Property Tax Assistance Law or the Senior Citizen Property Tax Postponement Law. (Impact Report, p.9–10; §4.58.030(C)(3))
Oversight: annual independent-audit review referred to a citizen oversight board (existing or new), designated by Council. (Impact Report, p.10; §4.58.080)
Vote threshold: simple majority (citizen-initiative case law), not two-thirds. (Impact Report, p.2)

title: Measure C
text:
Official Ballot Question (certified)

“Shall the measure to fund planning/construction/furnishing a new El Cerrito library, including a new building, and the City’s library operating costs for ten years after completing construction, by authorizing an annual parcel tax of up to $0.17 per square foot of improvements ($100 per vacant parcel), subject to annual inflation adjustments, generating approximately $3,100,000 annually, expiring 30 years after the initial issuance of bonds, with independent audits/citizen oversight and senior exemptions, be adopted?”


Source: contracostavote.gov/m9002-en, Impartial Analysis dated 3/12/2026.

title: Measure C
section: Financing Structure Assumed for the TOD Scenario (Scenario 3)
text:
Financing Structure Assumed for the TOD Scenario (Scenario 3)

Assumed bond: ~$37M, 30-year term, 5.00% interest → level annual debt service of $2,421,475. (Impact Report, p.19)
Current library annual operating/maintenance cost: $157,615, presently General-Fund-funded. (Impact Report, p.19)
Post-year-10 General Fund exposure: $187,755–$797,000/year depending on scenario, escalating thereafter. (Impact Report, p.19–20)
Developer’s (Related California’s) estimated cost to build the library shell: $8 million, per the Griffin Structures cost estimate — subject to final costs/negotiation. (Impact Report, p.31)
Ground lease: City pays BART $1/year, coterminous with Related’s ~99-year BART ground lease. (Impact Report, p.30)

title: Measure C
text:
Proponents / Yes Campaign

Committee for a Plaza Station Library (C4PSL) — organized citizen group behind the original petition drive.
Greg Lyman — former Mayor; treasurer, Committee for a Plaza Station Library.
Al (Alan C.) Miller — President, El Cerrito Library Foundation; public comment 11/20/2023.
Michael Fischer — City-designated Library Commissioner; Chair, Contra Costa County Library Commission.
Georgina Edwards — C4PSL member.
Gabe Quinto — Mayor (2026); longtime Councilmember; associated with Yes-side messaging.
Sky Woodruff — contract City Attorney; authored the official Impartial Analysis and the Impact Report’s legal interpretations.

title: Measure C
text:
Opponents / No Campaign

“Neighbors For a Better El Cerrito” — authored the official ballot argument against Measure C.
“No On The Library Tax” (nomoreforevertax.org) — cited the $80,000 election-timing cost and the $21M→$37M cost-disclosure gap.
Councilmember William Ktsanes — sole dissenting vote (2/19/2026) against placing the measure on the June ballot, on cost/fiscal-responsibility and turnout-democracy grounds.


Op-ed by Maria Pantelia and James Porter, East Bay Times, published April 17, 2026, characterizing the measure as asking voters to “write a blank check.”

title: Going-Concern Audits
text: A “going concern” opinion is an auditor’s formal statement of substantial doubt about a government’s ability to meet its financial obligations. El Cerrito’s CAFRs/ACFRs contain this language across a specific multi-year period, documented year by year below.

title: Going-Concern Audits
text:
FY2013 and FY2014

“The accompanying financial statements have been prepared in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America, which contemplate continuation of the City as a going concern. However, as of June 30, 2014, the General Fund’s unrestricted cash balance was only $1… Although the City continues to issue Tax Revenue Anticipation Notes to supplement cash temporarily during the fiscal year, if deficit spending continues, it reduces the likelihood that the City will be able to continue as a going concern.”


FY2014 CAFR, Independent Auditor’s Report, “Emphasis of Matters,” pages 2–3. Auditor: Maze & Associates. FY2013 CAFR contains substantially similar language (page 3); General Fund unrestricted cash represented under 5 days of expenditures that year; FY2014’s total citywide unrestricted cash was $40,384.

title: Going-Concern Audits
text:
FY2015 and FY2016
No going-concern language present in either year’s CAFR.

title: Going-Concern Audits
text:
FY2017 and FY2018

“The accompanying financial statements have been prepared assuming that the City will continue as a going concern. As discussed in Note 21 to the financial statements, the City’s General Fund has a very limited fund balance that indicates that the City may not be able to continue as a going concern. These conditions raise substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern…”


FY2017 and FY2018 CAFRs, Independent Auditor’s Report, “Emphasis of Matter Regarding Going Concern,” referencing Note 21. Auditor: Badawi and Associates, CPAs. FY2017 available fund balance: deficit $186,227. FY2018: deficit $2,233,507.

title: Going-Concern Audits
text:
FY2019

“The City’s unassigned fund balance in the General Fund was a deficit of $1,707,620, which represents a $525,887 improvement over… the prior fiscal year.”


FY2019 CAFR, Independent Auditor’s Report (“Emphasis of Matter Regarding Going Concern”) and Note 20, “GOING CONCERN.” Auditor: Badawi and Associates, CPAs (report dated January 31, 2020). Note: the auditor’s letter refers to “Note 21,” but the corresponding note in this year’s financial statements is numbered Note 20 — an apparent carryover drafting error from the prior year’s template, not a discrepancy in the underlying finding.

title: Going-Concern Audits
text:
FY2020

“The City’s unassigned fund balance in the General Fund was a deficit of $1,777,532.”


FY2020 CAFR, Independent Auditor’s Report (“Emphasis of Matter Regarding Going Concern”) and Note 21, “GOING CONCERN.” Auditor: Badawi & Associates. The FY2020 CAFR separately states elsewhere in its narrative that the City had been “on the going concern watch list since FY 2017, the first year that the City changed auditors in about a decade” — the City’s own characterization of the period.

title: Going-Concern Audits
text:
FY2021 — Going-Concern Language Discontinued

“As a result of the fund balance at 19% of estimated expenditures and a positive trend in both revenue and expenditures, the ‘Going Concern’ designation by Badawi and Associates is no longer included in the FY 2021 ACFR.”


FY2021 ACFR, Management’s Discussion and Analysis. Auditor: Badawi and Associates (same auditor as the prior four years; the going-concern designation ended before the subsequent auditor change).

title: Going-Concern Audits
text:
FY2022–FY2025

title: California State Auditor Findings
text:
In March 2021, the California State Auditor designated El Cerrito a “high risk” local government in Report 2020-803, titled “Excessive Spending and Insufficient Efforts to Address Its Perilous Financial Condition Jeopardize the City’s Ongoing Fiscal Viability.”
The audit found that El Cerrito spent more than it received in general fund revenue in eight of the eleven fiscal years from 2009–10 through 2019–20, and that its general fund reserves — built up to a peak of $2.6 million in FY2011–12 — were fully depleted by FY2016–17 and remained negative through FY2019–20. The city’s own reserve policy requires a minimum of 10% of expenditures; it did not meet that threshold in any of the eleven years reviewed.

Source: Report 2020-803, Table 1, based on the City’s audited comprehensive annual financial reports, FY2009–10 through FY2019–20. GFOA’s recommended minimum is 17% (two months of expenditures); El Cerrito’s own policy sets a 10% minimum.

The report also found the city relied on short-term loans (TRANs) every year since FY2012–13 to cover operating costs, with the loan amount growing from $5 million in FY2015–16 to a peak of $9 million in FY2019–20. The associated interest rate roughly doubled over that span, and annual interest costs more than tripled. The auditor’s own comparison noted that El Cerrito’s credit rating deteriorated from an AA− rating in 2016 to a BBB− rating in 2020, tracking the decline in reserves.
Other findings included a net pension liability of $65.8 million as of June 2020 (a 67% increase from FY2014–15), and a capital/maintenance backlog of $245.4 million identified in the FY2020–21 budget, of which only $21.4 million was funded through FY2024–25 — a rate the auditor noted would take more than 50 years to address at that pace. The audit also identified budget-monitoring weaknesses, including a finding that finance department staff routinely overrode internal spending-limit alerts without director-level review.

Source: California State Auditor, Report 2020-803, “City of El Cerrito: Excessive Spending and Insufficient Efforts to Address Its Perilous Financial Condition Jeopardize the City’s Ongoing Fiscal Viability,” issued March 16, 2021. Full report | City’s posted response page

title: Cost & Funding History
section: The Gap Between Internal Knowledge and Public Disclosure
text:
The Gap Between Internal Knowledge and Public Disclosure
The Impact Report itself states that the $37,224,000 Scenario 3 figure was finalized only after the January 20, 2026 study session and was not the number presented live at that meeting (Impact Report, p.24) — meaning the most current, precise cost figure was not made public until the February 19, 2026 Impact Report, roughly one month after the January 20 session and many months after the petition (using the ~$21.2M figure) had already been circulated and signed (petition filed November 20, 2025).
Whether City staff possessed a $37M-range estimate before the November 2025 petition filing is the central question in the “known but undisclosed” argument. The documented record supports: the City engaged Griffin Structures as Owner’s Representative starting April 1, 2025 — before the May 6, 2025 Notice of Intent, and well before the November 20, 2025 petition filing — specifically to provide updated TOD cost information.

Strongest documented evidence available: as of January 20, 2026, staff already had a $35–48M range in hand (Agenda Bill 8.B), well above the ~$21.2M petition figure. This range is dated to the Jan. 20, 2026 staff report; an earlier-dated internal document proving the City had this range specifically before the Nov. 20, 2025 petition filing has not been confirmed. Any public claim should be limited to what’s provable from dated documents, pending further records request.

title: Cost & Funding History
text:
Other Financing Facts

Special election cost commonly cited at $80,000 for the consolidated June 2 date. Per the Jan. 20, 2026 agenda bill, a standalone (non-consolidated) special election would have cost $213,768–$267,210, versus $3–4.50/registered voter (roughly $53,000–$80,000) if consolidated with the June 2 statewide primary — the $80,000 figure is the high end of the consolidated-election estimate, not the standalone cost. (Agenda Bill 8.A, 1/20/2026, p.1)
Tax collection start: per the Impact Report’s legal analysis, earliest realistic start was the 2026-27 tax year, with an Effective Date potentially as early as July 31, 2026 (Impact Report, p.11–12), contingent on County certification in time for the Council’s July 21, 2026 regular meeting. Actual tax bills (ad valorem mechanics) go out in the fall and are due December 10 / April 10 (Impact Report, p.12).
Comparable benchmark: current library’s existing annual operating/maintenance cost is $157,615 (Impact Report, p.19).

title: San Pablo Avenue Specific Plan & Complete Streets
text:
Project: C5035, “San Pablo Avenue Complete Streets” — implements the San Pablo Avenue Specific Plan and Complete Streets Plan, adopted by City Council in September 2014, in the Mid-town and Downtown sections.
Scope: sidewalk replacement, pedestrian-level lighting, crosswalk improvements (curb bulb-outs, pedestrian refuge islands, flashing lights, enhanced signing/striping), new mid-block crosswalks, bike facility implementation (route, lanes, cycletrack), bus islands, street trees, landscaping, and street furniture.
Status (FY2026-27/FY2027-28 budget): Planning. A 35% concept plan was completed in December 2020, funded by a Regional Measure 2 Safe Routes to Transit grant.
CEQA: cleared as part of the San Pablo Avenue Specific Plan & Complete Streets Plan FEIR, adopted September 2014.
Funding status: project is pending additional funding. Anticipated sources include the Active Transportation Program, the One Bay Area Grant Program, and CCTA Measure J TLC funds. A local match of $250,000 is budgeted in FY2031 for construction, contingent on a successful grant application.
Funding shown in the current biennial budget (all years): $250,000 (SB1 – Road Maintenance and Rehabilitation Account, FY2031 only) — a placeholder local-match amount, not a construction budget.

title: Richmond Street & Complete Streets
section: Thread C — AHSC Round 8 (executed grant, redirected)
text:
Thread C — AHSC Round 8 (executed grant, redirected)

Original grant: Agreement No. 24-AHSC-18468, “Parcel A South” — an east-west bikeway package: Central Ave (Class IV), Lincoln Ave (Class III), San Diego St/Belmont Ave (Class III), feeding into the Ohlone Greenway.
May 18, 2026: Public Works Director Yvetteh Ortiz requested deleting the Lincoln Ave segment (1.1 lane miles) and substituting Richmond St/Elm St (2.0 lane miles, Class II) + Central Ave (0.1 mi).
May 20, 2026, 9:28 AM: SGC’s A’shanti Coleman initially rejected the amendment (project scoring dropped from 4 to 1).
May 20, 2026, 2:46 PM: SGC’s Marc Caswell reversed that rejection the same day and approved it by email, citing a “lapse in reading comprehension.”

The pattern: after Thread B (money specifically earmarked for Richmond St bike lanes) was denied in December 2025, the City used the Thread C amendment (May 2026) to redirect a different AHSC grant — originally committed to a unique east-west connector (Lincoln Ave) — onto the same, previously-unfunded Richmond St corridor.
Richmond St runs roughly three blocks east of, and parallel to, the Ohlone Greenway (a Class I path running the full length of the city). The Richmond St segment covers only about one mile — largely redundant with that existing path.

Source: Public Works staff correspondence with SGC, May 18–20, 2026; SGC scoring records.

title: Richmond Street & Complete Streets
text:
Design Standard Concern
The Local Road Safety Plan (Kittelson, July 2026) states that physical separation is required on corridors with speeds above 25 mph. Richmond St exceeds this threshold by the City’s own data, but the project as designed uses paint-only Class II lanes, not physically separated Class IV. The LRSP explicitly excludes Richmond St from its own Backbone Bikeway analysis, deferring instead to the Complete Streets project.
CEQA Notice of Exemption (signed March 19, 2026 by Ortiz, for Thread A) already used the naming “Richmond St and Elm St, Key Blvd to Fairmount Ave” — a documented geographic link between Thread A and the Thread C amendment two months later.

Current Funding Picture (FY2026-27/FY2027-28 Biennial Budget)
The City’s Capital Improvement Program budget (Project C3080, “Richmond Street Complete Streets Improvement”) shows the following, current as of the FY2026-27/FY2027-28 biennial budget:
Project description in this budget document: “traffic calming features including chicanes, raised intersections, speed tables, and curb bulb-outs; pedestrian safety features…; enhanced bikeways, specifically bicycle lanes in each direction north of Moeser Lane…approximately 1.85 miles along Elm Street and Richmond Street between the Key Boulevard/Hill Street/Elm Street intersection and the Richmond Street/Fairmount Avenue/Ohlone Greenway intersection.” — the same 1.85-mile corridor as Thread A.
Narrative funding description (Pertinent Issues section): “The City entered into a Cooperative Agreement with the CCTA for CCTA to lead the project given the primary funding source is a Safe Streets for All funding for projects throughout the County.” — this still describes SS4A (Thread A) as the primary funding source.
Funding table (Detailed Breakdown), FY2027 requested:

The “$2,600,600 State Grant” line is itself broken out elsewhere in the same document as $1,800,600 from AHSC and $800,000 from SB1 LPP, per a March 2026 Council Report — no SS4A line item appears anywhere in this funding table.

This is a genuine, unresolved tension in the source documents, not something I’ve reconciled: the project’s own narrative section still names SS4A as the “primary funding source,” but the itemized funding table shows AHSC + SB1 LPP funding instead, with no SS4A line at all. One plausible explanation is that SS4A funds flow through CCTA’s own budget (since CCTA is leading that portion under the Cooperative Agreement) and simply don’t appear in the City’s own capital budget table, while the $4.35M shown here represents a separate, City-administered slice of the same overall project. That is a plausible reading, not a confirmed one. The March 2026 Council Report cited in this budget document has not yet been pulled and reviewed directly — that document would resolve this.

title: Richmond Street & Complete Streets
text:
Related: Nearby AHSC Round 10 Application (New)
Separately, the City’s Community Development Department FY2024-25/FY2025-26 accomplishments report states: “AHSC Round 10: requested approximately $3.5 million in Complete Streets improvements as part of the City’s AHSC Parcel C East application. Award announcement anticipated in December 2026.”
This reuses the “Parcel C East” name from the denied Thread B application (which sought ~$42.4M), but for a much smaller amount (~$3.5M). Whether this is a scaled-down resubmission of Thread B, a different phase, or something else has not been confirmed.

Source: FY2026-27/FY2027-28 Biennial Budget, Community Development Department accomplishments section.
